text: A few years later, he moved everyone back.
Then he had another idea.
He issued copper and brass coins, and declared them worth the same as silver.
Within months, people across the land were making coins at home, blacksmiths, farmers,
anyone with a furnace, piles of fake money.
The sultan had to buy them all back, with real silver.
money backed only by the state's promise. A great idea. About 500 years too early.
Then in 1398 the Central Asian conqueror Timur swept in and sacked Delhi. He took
its treasure, its craftsmen, even its elephants back to Samarkand. The city
took a century to recover. Remember Timur. His family isn't finished with India.
But here's what was happening while sultans came and went.
The newcomers were changing.
Persian and Indian builders mixed their styles in arches, domes, and minarets.
The poet Amir Khusrow wrote in a blend of Persian and the local speech, and is credited
with shaping kawali music.
And out of Delhi's bazaars and army camps, a whole new language grew, what would become
Urdu, the close cousin of Hindi.
Remember our question. They came as raiders. Within a few generations, they were eating
India's food, singing India's songs, and speaking a language that could only have been
born here.
Far to the south, a Hindu empire, Vijayanagara, was building a capital that foreign visitors
compared to Rome. Then, in 1526, a young prince rode down from Kabul. He had lost his kingdom
him more than once, and he was looking for a new one. On his father's side, he was the
great-great-great grandson of Timur.
